category: Degree adverbs that turn it down

examples: The movie was rather long, but I enjoyed it.
The instructions were rather confusing.
She talked rather quickly, so I missed a few words.
I'd rather stay home tonight.
Would you rather have tea or coffee?
I'd rather you didn't tell anyone.
She's my cousin — or rather, my second cousin.
We left at six, or rather a little after six.
The problem isn't the price. Rather, it's the long wait.
He didn't calm down; rather, he got even angrier.
The goal is not to win the argument but rather to understand the other side.

senses.head: To a fairly large degree; quite, often more than expected
examples: The movie was rather long, but I enjoyed it.
The instructions were rather confusing.
She talked rather quickly, so I missed a few words.

senses.head: Used with would ('d rather) to say what someone prefers
examples: I'd rather stay home tonight.
Would you rather have tea or coffee?
I'd rather you didn't tell anyone.

senses.head: More exactly; used after or to correct or refine what was just said
examples: She's my cousin — or rather, my second cousin.
We left at six, or rather a little after six.

senses.head: Instead; on the contrary — introducing the true situation after a negative statement
examples: The problem isn't the price. Rather, it's the long wait.
He didn't calm down; rather, he got even angrier.
The goal is not to win the argument but rather to understand the other side.

entries.type: degree; also linking (rather 'instead') and preference in would rather
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective, adverb or comparative (rather long, rather better); mid in would rather; front in the 'instead' sense
entries.modifies: adjectives, adverbs, comparatives, verbs of liking (I rather like it), and a/an + adjective + noun (rather a long time)
entries.contrast: In American speech rather 'quite' sounds formal or British; everyday American English says pretty or kind of (pretty cold). Would rather takes a bare infinitive — I'd rather go, not I'd rather to go — and a past-tense clause about someone else (I'd rather you stayed). Rather than (walk rather than drive) works as a conjunction or preposition and is covered there. Russian скорее also means 'sooner, faster' — that is sooner or faster, never rather.

entries.meaning: To some degree but not very much; a little. ---
examples: I was somewhat surprised by her answer.
Prices have fallen somewhat since last year.
The second edition is somewhat longer than the first.
entries.type: degree — a downtoner, more formal than kind of or sort of
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives, adverbs and comparatives; end or mid with verbs (It helped somewhat)
entries.contrast: Russian несколько means both 'somewhat' and 'several' — несколько устал is somewhat tired, and several never modifies an adjective. Somewhat does not stand before a noun: say a somewhat odd idea. Somewhat of a (somewhat of a surprise) is a pronoun use that careful writers replace with something of a or a bit of a.

examples: The new version is slightly faster.
I'm slightly worried about the weather.
The price went up slightly in March.
He was a quiet, slightly built man in his fifties.
She is slightly built but surprisingly strong.

senses.head: A little; to a small degree
examples: The new version is slightly faster.
I'm slightly worried about the weather.
The price went up slightly in March.

senses.head: In a slim, small way — used of how a person is built
examples: He was a quiet, slightly built man in his fifties.
She is slightly built but surprisingly strong.

entries.position: before its word — before adjectives, adverbs and comparatives; mid or end with verbs
entries.modifies: adjectives, comparatives, adverbs, verbs, and the participle built
entries.contrast: Slightly modifies adjectives and verbs, never a noun: slightly different, a slight difference, not slightly difference. Russian немного before a noun is a little (a little money), not slightly. 'Not at all' is not in the slightest, not not slightly.

examples: The show was only moderately successful.
Most of the rooms are moderately priced.
Stir in the flour and cook over moderately high heat.
He drinks only moderately — a glass of wine with dinner, at most.
Exercise moderately at first and build up slowly.

senses.head: To a medium degree; fairly but not very
examples: The show was only moderately successful.
Most of the rooms are moderately priced.
Stir in the flour and cook over moderately high heat.

senses.head: Without going to extremes; within reasonable limits
examples: He drinks only moderately — a glass of wine with dinner, at most.
Exercise moderately at first and build up slowly.

entries.русский: умеренно, в меру, в средней степени
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives and participles (moderately priced); end in the 'within limits' sense (drink moderately)
entries.comparison: more/most — more moderately priced, eat more moderately
entries.form: -ly from the adjective moderate, pronounced MAHD-ur-uht — not like the verb moderate (MAHD-uh-rayt)
entries.contrast: Before an adjective moderately is faint praise: moderately successful means 'so-so', not 'quite successful'. For eating and drinking the everyday phrase is in moderation (drink in moderation); moderately sounds more clinical.

examples: It'll be partly cloudy tomorrow, with a chance of showers.
The door was partly open.
What she said is only partly true.
I moved to Denver partly for the job and partly to be near my sister.
The delay was partly my fault.
Sales fell, partly because of the bad weather.

senses.head: Not completely; to some extent
examples: It'll be partly cloudy tomorrow, with a chance of showers.
The door was partly open.
What she said is only partly true.

senses.head: Used to give one reason or cause among several
examples: I moved to Denver partly for the job and partly to be near my sister.
The delay was partly my fault.
Sales fell, partly because of the bad weather.

entries.position: before its word — before adjectives, noun phrases and because or due to; mid with verbs (it partly explains)
entries.modifies: adjectives, participles, verbs, noun phrases (partly my fault), and reason phrases
entries.contrast: Partly and partially overlap in 'not completely', but for reasons and in the pair partly... partly American usage prefers partly (partly because, not partially because); for a physical, unfinished state partially is common (partially cooked). Both Russian частично and отчасти translate partly; for отчасти with a reason, use partly.

examples: The road is partially closed for repairs.
He is partially deaf in one ear.
Add the partially cooked pasta to the sauce.
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives and participles; mid with verbs (has partially recovered)
entries.contrast: The adjective partial also means 'biased' and 'fond of' (partial to chocolate), but partially today means only 'not completely' — an American reader takes judged partially as 'judged in part'. For 'with bias' say unfairly or with bias; the old sense lives on only in impartially. For reasons use partly, not partially (partly because).

examples: I could barely keep my eyes open.
She barely passed the exam.
There was barely enough food for everyone.
We had barely sat down when the phone rang.
She had barely started the new job when the company shut down.
Barely had the game started when it began to rain.

senses.head: Only just; almost not
examples: I could barely keep my eyes open.
She barely passed the exam.
There was barely enough food for everyone.

senses.head: Only a very short time before; just
examples: We had barely sat down when the phone rang.
She had barely started the new job when the company shut down.
Barely had the game started when it began to rain.

entries.type: degree — a downtoner with negative force; also time
entries.position: mid — before the main verb, after be and the first auxiliary; front with inversion in literary style
entries.modifies: verbs, adjectives, quantifiers and numbers (barely enough, barely 20 people)
entries.form: -ly from bare, but not its meaning (bare = naked, uncovered)
entries.contrast: Barely is already negative, so never add not: I can barely hear, not I can't barely hear; tag questions are positive (She barely knows him, does she?). The time pattern is barely... when, not than (than goes with no sooner). Fronted Barely needs inversion: Barely had we arrived when it started to rain. Russian едва ли means 'unlikely' — that is hardly likely or probably not, not barely.

examples: Dinner's almost ready.
Almost everyone came to the meeting.
She almost always takes the bus.
I almost missed the flight.
He slipped on the ice and almost fell.

senses.head: Not quite; very nearly
examples: Dinner's almost ready.
Almost everyone came to the meeting.
She almost always takes the bus.

senses.head: Used with a past verb for something that very nearly happened but did not
examples: I almost missed the flight.
He slipped on the ice and almost fell.

entries.position: mid — before the main verb (I almost fell); before its word with adjectives, numbers, all, every, no and always
entries.modifies: verbs, adjectives, adverbs, numbers, and quantifiers (almost all, almost nobody)
entries.contrast: Almost is not a determiner: almost all people or most people, never almost people, and almost all of us, not almost of us. Almost and nearly are close, but only almost goes with negative words (almost nothing, almost never, not nearly nothing), and only nearly takes very or not (very nearly, not nearly enough). For 'я чуть не упал' say I almost fell — no negative, not I almost didn't fall.

examples: The stadium was practically empty by the fourth quarter.
She practically begged me to come.
It costs practically nothing.
We need to think practically about the budget.
Try to look at the problem practically, not emotionally.
Practically speaking, we can't finish before Friday.
The idea is fine in theory, but practically it won't work.

senses.head: Almost; very nearly
examples: The stadium was practically empty by the fourth quarter.
She practically begged me to come.
It costs practically nothing.

senses.head: In a sensible, realistic way
examples: We need to think practically about the budget.
Try to look at the problem practically, not emotionally.

senses.head: In practice; from a practical point of view
examples: Practically speaking, we can't finish before Friday.
The idea is fine in theory, but practically it won't work.

entries.position: before its word — before adjectives, quantifiers and verbs; end in the 'sensibly' sense (think practically); front as a viewpoint adverb (Practically speaking)
entries.comparison: more/most — only in the 'sensibly' sense (think more practically); not gradable as 'almost'
entries.modifies: adjectives, verbs, quantifiers (practically everyone), and whole clauses
entries.form: -ly from practical; the -al- is usually swallowed (PRAK-tik-lee)
entries.contrast: As 'almost' practically is informal — in formal writing use almost or virtually. It can be ambiguous: practically impossible usually means 'almost impossible' but may mean 'impossible in practice', just like Russian практически. 'Practical, sensible' about a person is the adjective practical, not practically.

examples: It's virtually impossible to get a table there on a Saturday.
Virtually all of the tickets have been sold.
The two phones are virtually identical.
The conference will be held virtually this year.
You can tour the museum virtually from home.

senses.head: Almost completely; for all practical purposes
examples: It's virtually impossible to get a table there on a Saturday.
Virtually all of the tickets have been sold.
The two phones are virtually identical.

senses.head: Online or by computer, not in person
examples: The conference will be held virtually this year.
You can tour the museum virtually from home.

entries.position: before its word — before adjectives, quantifiers and verbs; end in the 'online' sense (meet virtually)
entries.modifies: adjectives, verbs, quantifiers (virtually everyone), and phrases (virtually overnight)
entries.contrast: In most texts virtually means 'almost', not виртуально: virtually unknown is 'почти неизвестный'. Only when it says how something is done — meet virtually, held virtually, tour virtually — does it mean 'online'. Russian фактически in the sense 'in fact' is actually or in fact, not virtually.

examples: Are you old enough to drive?
She didn't run fast enough to catch the bus.
I didn't sleep enough last night.
He's nice enough, but I wouldn't lend him money.
She sings well enough, but she'll never be a star.
Being a new parent is tiring enough without a two-hour commute.
Things are hard enough without you making jokes.
It's bad enough that we lost — now the bus has broken down.
Strangely enough, I'd never been to the ocean before.
I said it would rain, and sure enough, it poured.

senses.head: To the necessary degree; sufficiently
examples: Are you old enough to drive?
She didn't run fast enough to catch the bus.
I didn't sleep enough last night.

senses.head: Fairly or reasonably, but not especially — often followed by but
examples: He's nice enough, but I wouldn't lend him money.
She sings well enough, but she'll never be a star.

senses.head: Already quite — stressing that something is bad or hard even without anything more
examples: Being a new parent is tiring enough without a two-hour commute.
Things are hard enough without you making jokes.
It's bad enough that we lost — now the bus has broken down.

senses.head: After sure and some -ly stance adverbs, showing how the speaker sees a fact
examples: Strangely enough, I'd never been to the ocean before.
I said it would rain, and sure enough, it poured.

entries.type: degree — sets a sufficient level; also stance (oddly enough)
entries.position: after its word — after adjectives, adverbs and verbs (old enough, slept enough)
entries.modifies: adjectives, adverbs, and verbs; a following to-infinitive or for phrase gives the purpose
entries.contrast: The adverb follows its word: old enough, not enough old — Russian достаточно взрослый puts it first. Before a noun enough is a determiner and comes first: enough money, enough time. With adjective + noun it goes after the adjective: a big enough room. The purpose follows with to or for: old enough to vote, warm enough for a swim. I've had enough (pronoun) and Enough! (interjection) are other word classes.

entries.meaning: Fairly, when compared with other things or with what is usual. ---
examples: The apartment is relatively cheap for this part of town.
Relatively few people showed up.
Relatively speaking, it was a mild winter.
entries.type: degree — a downtoner that implies a comparison
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives, adverbs and few, little, small
entries.contrast: Russian относительно also means 'concerning' (относительно вашего письма) — that is regarding or about, never relatively. 'In relation to' is relative to (expensive relative to its size), not relatively to. Don't pair it with a comparative: relatively cheap, not relatively cheaper than.

examples: The food was reasonably good, and the service was fast.
Everything in the store is reasonably priced.
I'm reasonably sure the office closes at five.
Let's discuss this reasonably, without shouting.
She reacted very reasonably when I told her about the dent in her car.
If you'd acted more reasonably, we wouldn't be here.
You can reasonably expect a reply within a week.
No one could reasonably blame her for leaving.

senses.head: Fairly; to a satisfactory or acceptable degree
examples: The food was reasonably good, and the service was fast.
Everything in the store is reasonably priced.
I'm reasonably sure the office closes at five.

senses.head: In a sensible or fair way
examples: Let's discuss this reasonably, without shouting.
She reacted very reasonably when I told her about the dent in her car.
If you'd acted more reasonably, we wouldn't be here.

senses.head: With good reason; justifiably
examples: You can reasonably expect a reply within a week.
No one could reasonably blame her for leaving.

entries.position: before its word — before adjectives and participles (reasonably priced); end in the 'sensibly' sense; mid after a modal (can reasonably expect)
entries.comparison: more/most — more reasonably priced, behave more reasonably
entries.contrast: Before an adjective reasonably is a downtoner, not разумно: reasonably good means 'fairly good', and reasonably priced means 'not too expensive'. The sense 'justifiably' comes after a modal: can reasonably expect, could reasonably argue.

examples: The job pays comparatively well for the area.
The disease is comparatively rare in children.
Comparatively speaking, we were lucky.
The two languages are studied comparatively in the second semester.
The data were analyzed comparatively across five countries.

senses.head: Fairly, when compared with others or with what is usual
examples: The job pays comparatively well for the area.
The disease is comparatively rare in children.
Comparatively speaking, we were lucky.

senses.head: By means of comparison — in study and research
examples: The two languages are studied comparatively in the second semester.
The data were analyzed comparatively across five countries.

entries.type: degree — a downtoner that implies a comparison; also manner
entries.position: before its word — before adjectives and adverbs; end in the 'by comparison' sense (studied comparatively)
entries.modifies: adjectives, adverbs, and verbs of study
entries.contrast: The stress is on the second syllable: kuhm-PAIR-uh-tiv-lee, not KAHM-pur-. Like relatively, it already implies a comparison, so it takes the plain adjective: comparatively cheap, not comparatively cheaper; the standard follows with compared with or compared to (cheap compared with New York), not than.

examples: I was mildly surprised that she agreed.
The movie was mildly entertaining at best.
The salsa is only mildly spicy.
“That's not quite right,” she said mildly.
He complained mildly about the noise and went back to bed.
The meeting didn't go well, to put it mildly.
Her boss was upset, to put it mildly.

senses.head: Slightly; to a small degree
examples: I was mildly surprised that she agreed.
The movie was mildly entertaining at best.
The salsa is only mildly spicy.

senses.head: In a gentle, calm way; not harshly
examples: “That's not quite right,” she said mildly.
He complained mildly about the noise and went back to bed.

senses.head: In to put it mildly: saying that the reality is stronger than your words
examples: The meeting didn't go well, to put it mildly.
Her boss was upset, to put it mildly.

entries.position: before its word — before adjectives and participles; end in the 'gently' sense (she said mildly)
entries.modifies: adjectives, participles, and verbs of speaking and reacting
entries.contrast: To put it mildly is fixed — not to say it mildly — and signals understatement: upset, to put it mildly means 'very upset'. Russian мягко about touch or sound is softly or gently (close the door gently, speak softly); mildly is about tone and degree.

examples: Sales were marginally higher than last year.
Interest rates rose marginally in June.
This model is marginally cheaper, but the battery is worse.
The business is only marginally profitable.
His comments were marginally relevant at best.

senses.head: Very slightly; by a small amount
examples: Sales were marginally higher than last year.
Interest rates rose marginally in June.
This model is marginally cheaper, but the battery is worse.

senses.head: Only just; to a limited, borderline degree
examples: The business is only marginally profitable.
His comments were marginally relevant at best.

entries.position: before its word — before adjectives and comparatives; end with verbs (rose marginally)
entries.modifies: comparatives, adjectives, and verbs of change
entries.contrast: Russian маргинальный suggests people on the edge of society; English marginally just means 'slightly' or 'only just' — marginally better is 'чуть лучше'. It is formal; in speech Americans say a little or slightly.
